# Draft:Traditional ships (Germany)

Traditional ships in Germany (German: Traditionsschiffe) are a legally defined category of historic vessel under German maritime law. Under the German Ship Safety Ordinance (Schiffssicherheitsverordnung, SchSV), a traditional ship is a historic watercraft whose preservation and presentation while under way is considered to be in the public interest. The category is intended to preserve maritime heritage by allowing historically significant vessels to remain in operation under a dedicated safety and manning regime.
In German licence law, traditional ships are subject to specific rules on nautical qualifications. Depending on hull length, voyage area and the number of persons on board, a vessel may be operated either under the rules for yachts or under the specific provisions for traditional ships laid down in the Sportseeschifferscheinverordnung (SportSeeSchV).
Legal definition
The Ship Safety Ordinance defines traditional ships as historic watercraft, or their replicas, up to 55 metres in length, whose preservation and presentation while under way is in the public interest, especially for cultural reasons, and whose restoration and operation according to traditional seamanship serves the preservation of maritime heritage. For the purposes of the safety regime, the SchSV further describes a traditional ship as a historic watercraft built predominantly from original materials and preserved because of its type, construction, former use and rarity, and corresponding substantially either to its original state or to a historically significant later state from its working life.
Scope
Under German law, the special traditional-ship regime applies to vessels up to 55 metres in hull length. The SchSV contains a distinct set of technical, operational and safety requirements for traditional ships, separate from the rules for ordinary passenger ships, cargo ships and pleasure craft.
Traditional ships are not intended to function as ordinary commercial vessels. Their operation must serve idealistic, educational and heritage-preservation purposes, especially the communication of traditional seamanship and historic ship operation.
Certification
A traditional ship requires a safety certificate under German ship safety law. In the wording of the Sportseeschifferscheinverordnung, only vessels that have been issued a safety certificate on the basis of the safety guideline for traditional ships qualify as Traditionsschiffe for the purposes of that regulation.
The certificate is issued only where the vessel satisfies the legal definition and the applicable safety requirements. Recognition as a traditional ship is therefore linked not only to historical authenticity but also to compliance with an approved operational and safety concept.
Licensing
General framework
The licensing rules for traditional ships are laid down in the Sportseeschifferscheinverordnung (SportSeeSchV). The regulation distinguishes between yachts and traditional ships primarily according to hull length and the number of persons on board.
For the purposes of licensing, the requirements relate to the qualification of the person acting as master (Schiffsführer) of the vessel.
Vessels up to 25 metres
Traditional ships with a hull length of less than 15 metres and not more than 25 persons on board are treated as yachts. In such cases, operation within the seaward scope requires the appropriate recreational boating licence (Sportbootführerschein See).
If a traditional ship of less than 15 metres carries more than 25 persons on board, or if the vessel has a hull length of 15 to 25 metres, the qualification requirements follow the provisions for traditional ships. In coastal and near-shore sea waters, the master must hold a Sportseeschifferschein (SSS), while for worldwide navigation a Sporthochseeschifferschein (SHS) is required.
Vessels from 25 to 55 metres
For traditional ships with a hull length from 25 to 55 metres, the master must hold either an SSS (for coastal and near-shore sea waters) or an SHS (for worldwide navigation), in each case with a mandatory additional endorsement for traditional ships (Zusatzeintrag) under the SportSeeSchV.
In practice, this additional endorsement is often referred to colloquially as a Traditionsschifferschein, although legally it constitutes an extension of the SSS or SHS rather than a separate licence category.
A holder of the relevant certificate with this endorsement may operate traditional ships up to 55 metres in hull length within the voyage areas covered by the underlying SSS or SHS.
Manning
The SportSeeSchV also lays down principles for the manning of traditional ships. Responsibility for safe manning lies with the owner or operator, and crew members must hold the required certificates of competence or possess sufficient practical experience where no formal certificate is prescribed.
For traditional ships over 15 metres and up to 55 metres, the regulation provides for a standard manning table (Regelbesatzung) differentiated by hull length and voyage area.
Heritage role
Traditional ships occupy an intermediate position between museum ships and active seagoing vessels. Unlike static exhibits, they are expected to demonstrate historical maritime practice in operation. German law therefore combines the preservation of authenticity with enforceable standards on certification, operation, safety and manning.
